content.text:
I've studied the target site closely. It's built on a **Tufte/Edward-Tufte-style minimalist design** (same lineage as Tufte-CSS / Gwern.net), exported from Hugo. Key concrete specs I extracted from its actual CSS:

**Typography**
- Body: Alegreya (serif), weight 440, `1.4rem`/`2rem` line-height
- Headings (h1/h2) + bylines/tags: Alegreya SC (small caps, lowercase-forced via `text-transform`)
- Nav: Alegreya, uppercase, letterspaced
- Code: Inconsolata monospace

**Layout**
- Centered content column, max-width `1080px`, but `main`/`footer` have `margin-right: 26rem` — that's the trick: a wide right margin reserved for **sidenotes** (`.side`, figcaption, captions) which float right into that margin (`margin-right: -24rem; width: 21rem`), Tufte-style — footnotes and figures live beside the text instead of at the bottom
- h1 gets a centered SVG ornament above it (masked, so it recolors with the CSS var)
- Small ornament divider before "Read Next" / "Subscribe" sections (`§` section markers)
- KaTeX for math

**Color (light / dark via `prefers-color-scheme`)**
- Light: bg `#fcfcfc`, text `#111`, link `#003366`, accent `#660000`, border `#ccc`
- Dark: bg `#16161a`, text `#d6d6d6`, link `#8cb4e8`, accent `#e0928c`

**Structure**: flat nav (Home/About/Posts/RSS), posts listed as date → tags → title → one-line description, "Read Next" and "Subscribe" as its own `§`-marked sections, minimal footer with license/copyright.

Your current site is a Jekyll/Poole-Hyde theme with a full business-site IA (Services, Leistungen, Case Studies, Certifications, Projects, Articles/de-Artikel...) plus a `/blog/` section — quite different in scope from a personal Tufte-style blog.

## Design Draft: Tufte-style Blog/Articles Redesign **Scope:** `_layouts/article.html`, `_layouts/post.html`, `articles/index.html`, `de/artikel/index.md`, `blog/index.html` (and their partials). Everything else (Services, Leistungen, Case Studies, etc.) stays as-is. ### 1. Typography | Role | Current | New | |---|---|---| | Body text | Lora | **Alegreya** (serif), weight ~440, `font-size: 1.05rem`, `line-height: 1.9` | | Headings (h1/h2) | Cormorant Garamond | **Alegreya SC** small-caps, lowercase-forced, letterspaced | | Nav / meta | Inter | Alegreya, uppercase, letterspaced (small-caps energy without the SC face) | | Code | — | Inconsolata / existing mono stack | Fonts self-hosted via `@font-face` + `size-adjust` fallback trick (same pattern as source) so there's no layout shift — I'll add `Alegreya` + `Alegreya SC` woff2 files under `/public/fonts/`. ### 2. Color tokens (CSS custom properties, auto light/dark) ``` --bg: #fcfcfc --bg (dark): #16161a --text: #111 --text (dark): #d6d6d6 --link: #003366 --link (dark): #8cb4e8 --accent: #660000 --accent (dark): #e0928c --border: #ccc --border (dark): #3a3a3a ``` Switches via `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, scoped to `.article-body`/`.blog` containers only so it doesn't leak into the business pages. ### 3. Layout: sidenotes The source reserves a `26rem` right margin and floats footnotes/captions into it (`.side`, `width: 21rem`, `margin-right: -24rem`). # Alex Snow — AI & LLM Consultant

## Overview
AI and LLM consulting for SMBs and cultural institutions (museums, galleries, archives). Specialising in practical GenAI applications, MLOps, and agentic systems — from strategy to production.

**URL:** https://alexsnow348.github.io
**Author:** Alex Snow (Wuthmoneh Ninhlaing)
**Location:** Germany (DACH region)
**Languages:** English, German (elementary), Burmese (native)

## Professional Focus
- AI Strategy & Roadmapping for German Mittelstand
- LLM Application Development (RAG, chatbots, document intelligence)
- Agentic Workflow Design (multi-agent systems, automation)
- MLOps & Model Deployment (Databricks, Azure ML, MLflow)
- GenAI for Cultural Institutions (collection cataloguing, provenance research, visitor engagement)

## Background
- MLOps Architect at ControlExpert GmbH (2026–present)
- MLOps Engineer at LPKF Laser & Electronics SE (2023–2026)
- Lead Back End / ML Engineer at TM Research & Development, Malaysia (2017–2023)
- M.Sc. Data Analytics, Stiftung Universität Hildesheim (2023–2025)
- Founder, Alex Snow School — award-winning AI/ML education initiative for Myanmar youth
- 81+ professional certifications across Coursera, Databricks, Udacity, IBM, and others
- Winner, Falling Walls Lab Myanmar 2020

## Site Sections
- /about/ — Full professional background, experience, education, certifications
- /services/ — Consulting services for SMBs and cultural institutions (English)
- /leistungen/ — Consulting services in German (KMU & Kultureinrichtungen)
- /articles/ — English articles on GenAI applications in art and museum contexts
- /de/artikel/ — German translations of the same GenAI × museum articles
- /case-studies/ — Anonymised project case studies across automotive, industrial, telecom, and cultural sectors
- /own-certifications/ — Searchable list of 81+ certifications with filters
- /projects/ — Community and technical projects (2017–2022)
- /talks/ — Public talks on AI, ML, and career development

## Articles (English, AI × Art & Museum)
Each includes a "Key Takeaways" summary and an FAQ section for quick reference.
- "How GenAI Is Transforming Museum Collection Cataloguing" — metadata enrichment, vision-language models, RAG pipelines, EU data residency
- "RAG Systems for Provenance Research: Making Restitution Archives Searchable" — Nazi-era art displacement records, Fraktur OCR, semantic retrieval
- "Multilingual Visitor Chatbots for German Museums: What Actually Works" — RAG-grounded chatbots, multilingual output, scoping and economics
- "Starting With AI When You Have No Tech Team: A Guide for Small German Museums" — practical first steps, off-the-shelf tools, scoping for small institutions

## Artikel (Deutsch, KI × Kunst & Museum)
Vollständige deutsche Übersetzungen der vier englischen Artikel, jeweils mit "Das Wichtigste in Kürze" und FAQ-Abschnitt, unter /de/artikel/.

## Case Studies
- Industrial: Computer vision QA pipeline for precision manufacturing (Germany)
- Telecom: AI-driven network diagnostics reducing helpdesk resolution from 27h to 9h
- Cultural: GenAI collection cataloguing for a regional museum (Germany)

## Contact
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/wuthmonehninhlaing/

RAG makes provenance archives queryable in natural language, replacing manual cross-referencing across scattered documents.

content.text:
## Root cause found and fixed

The Google Fonts `<link>` in `_includes/head.html` bundled a self-hosted font (`century-burma`) into the same `fonts.googleapis.com/css2` query as the real Google Fonts. Google Fonts rejects the **entire request** (HTTP 400) when one family name in the query is invalid — so *none* of the fonts were loading, old or new. Every page was silently falling back to the browser's default serif, which is why the Alegreya/Alegreya SC change appeared to have no effect.

**Fixed:**
- Removed `century-burma` from the Google Fonts query string (it's already self-hosted separately via `@font-face` in `public/css/main.scss` and used via a dedicated `.myanmar-text` style — untouched, still works)
- Verified the corrected URL now returns `200 OK`
- Enlarged the ornament divider (`11rem × 1.3rem` → `19rem × 2.2rem`)

Both changes are in `_includes/head.html` and `_scss/component/_tufte.scss`, build verified clean. Once you reload with a hard refresh (or restart your local server), Alegreya/Alegreya SC should actually render now.

AI × Art & Museum

How GenAI Is Transforming Museum Collection Cataloguing

May 8, 2026 6 min read GenAI, Collections, RAG, Metadata

Most museum collections are sitting on decades of inconsistent metadata — free-text descriptions, staff abbreviations, missing fields, and records that exist only in physical ledgers. The traditional answer has been slow, expensive manual cataloguing. GenAI changes the equation.

Key takeaways:

  • Vision-language models can turn object photographs into structured draft metadata — material, technique, period, condition — for curator review, not curator replacement.
  • LLM pipelines can normalise decades of inconsistent free-text records into standardised fields, flagging ambiguous entries for human review instead of guessing.
  • RAG makes provenance archives queryable in natural language, replacing manual cross-referencing across scattered documents.
  • Start with a bounded pilot of 500–2,000 objects, keep a human-in-the-loop review step, and check EU data residency requirements before choosing a model provider.

The Scale of the Problem

Germany alone has over 6,800 cultural institutions. The Staatliche Museen zu Berlin holds over five million objects. The Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg — another three million. For smaller regional museums, even a collection of 20,000 objects can represent decades of backlogged cataloguing work, because most institutions lack the curatorial staff to keep pace.

The result: objects sit in storage, undiscoverable to researchers and the public alike. What can’t be searched can’t be studied — or lent, or digitised, or made accessible.

What GenAI Actually Does Here

Generative AI doesn’t replace curators. It handles the labour-intensive groundwork so curators can focus on interpretation and context.

Metadata enrichment from image input. Current-generation vision-language models (Claude, GPT-5, Gemini) can analyse high-resolution photographs of objects and produce structured draft records — material, technique, period estimation, iconographic elements, condition notes. A curator reviews and confirms rather than writes from scratch.

Normalising legacy records. Decades of free-text descriptions can be processed through an LLM pipeline to extract and standardise fields: creator, date range, provenance, dimensions, acquisition source. The model flags ambiguous entries for human review rather than guessing.

Multilingual metadata generation. For institutions targeting international researchers or tourists, GenAI can generate German, English, and French metadata variants from a single authoritative record — consistent in tone and accurate in terminology.

RAG-powered provenance research. Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems can make thousands of scanned auction records, dealer invoices, and correspondence queryable. A curator asks “show me all records referencing Galerie Flechtheim between 1925 and 1933” — the system retrieves and surfaces relevant fragments across digitised archives. I go into this in more depth in my piece on RAG for provenance research.

A Realistic Implementation Path

The gap between a proof-of-concept and production-ready cataloguing pipeline is significant. A few principles that hold across institutions I’ve worked with:

  1. Start with a bounded collection. Pick 500–2,000 objects with reasonable existing records. Use these to calibrate the model’s output quality and establish a review workflow before scaling.

  2. Build a human-in-the-loop review step. No AI output should go directly to a public-facing catalogue. The value is in reducing the curator’s time-per-object from 45 minutes to 10, not in removing the curator.

  3. Define your controlled vocabulary first. GenAI will generate inconsistent terminology unless constrained. Feeding your institution’s preferred vocabulary (Getty AAT, for example) as context dramatically improves consistency.

  4. Data residency matters in Germany. GDPR and institutional data policies often require that collection data — especially provenance records — not leave EU infrastructure. Azure OpenAI, Mistral, and German-hosted alternatives are worth evaluating alongside US-based APIs.

What This Enables Beyond Cataloguing

A well-structured digital collection is not just a curatorial asset — it’s infrastructure. Once metadata is consistent and machine-readable, you can:

  • Power semantic search for researchers (find by concept, not just keyword)
  • Generate accessible image descriptions for visually impaired visitors
  • Build multilingual visitor chatbots grounded in your own collection data
  • Surface collection items relevant to temporary exhibitions automatically

The backlog is the bottleneck. GenAI makes clearing it tractable.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can GenAI replace museum curators for cataloguing?

No. It handles the labour-intensive groundwork — draft descriptions, field normalisation, translation — while curators review, correct, and add interpretation. The goal is reducing time-per-object, not removing curatorial judgement.

Which AI models can generate metadata from object photographs?

Current-generation vision-language models such as Claude, GPT-5, and Gemini can analyse high-resolution images and produce structured draft records, though every output still needs curatorial review before publication.

Does collection data have to leave the EU to use GenAI?

No — GDPR and institutional policy often require EU data residency for provenance records, so Azure OpenAI, Mistral, and other EU-hosted options are worth evaluating alongside US-based APIs.

How big should a first cataloguing pilot be?

500–2,000 objects with reasonably complete existing records — enough to calibrate output quality and build a review workflow before scaling to the full collection.

If your institution has no in-house tech team at all, start here for a lower-lift path in.

how do i differnt it is english or burmese post

The site differentiates by a `lang` front-matter field on each post:

```yaml
---
layout: post
title: "..."
lang: en        # or lang: de
---
```

- **Has `lang: en` or `lang: de`** → treated as English/German: gets the new Tufte styling (Alegreya/Alegreya SC serif, small-caps headings, sidenote-margin byline)
- **No `lang` field at all** → treated as Burmese by default: gets Padauk font, and shows up in the "Burmese" section on the homepage and gets the `lang-my` class in the blog listing/read-next

This is checked in a few places: `_layouts/post.html` (`unless page.lang`), `index.html` (`p.lang != nil` vs `p.lang == nil`), and `blog/index.html`/`_includes/read-next.html` (same `unless post.lang` pattern).

**So to make a post English:** add `lang: en` to its front matter. **To make it Burmese:** just leave `lang` out — that's already the convention for all ~100 existing Burmese posts.

One caveat worth knowing: this relies on absence-of-field, so if you ever write a new English post and forget to add `lang: en`, it'll silently render in Padauk with the Burmese font/section instead. If you want it more robust, I could flip the logic to require an explicit `lang: my` on Burmese posts instead — but that means touching front matter on ~100 files. Want me to do that, or is the current convention fine to keep working with?

import re, glob, sys

EMOJI = re.compile(
    '['
    '\U0001F300-\U0001FAFF'
    '\U00002600-\U000027BF'
    '\U0001F1E6-\U0001F1FF'
    '\U00002B00-\U00002BFF'
    '\U0000FE0F'
    '\U0000200D'
    ']', flags=re.UNICODE)

def clean_line(line, in_code):
    if not EMOJI.search(line):
        return line, False
    new = EMOJI.sub('', line)
    if not in_code:
        # collapse runs of 2+ spaces (but keep leading indentation)
        stripped_leading = len(new) - len(new.lstrip(' '))
        lead = new[:stripped_leading]
        rest = new[stripped_leading:]
        rest = re.sub(r' {2,}', ' ', rest)
        new = lead + rest
    return new, True

changed_files = []
for f in sorted(glob.glob('_posts/*.md')):
    with open(f, encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        text = fh.read()
    lines = text.split('\n')
    out = []
    in_code = False
    any_change = False
    for line in lines:
        if line.strip().startswith('```'):
            in_code = not in_code
        new_line, changed = clean_line(line, in_code)
        if changed:
            any_change = True
        out.append(new_line)
    if any_change:
        new_text = '\n'.join(out)
        # fix title line quote spacing: title: " X" -> title: "X", title: "X " -> title: "X"
        new_text = re.sub(
            r'^title:\s*"(.*?)"\s*$',
            lambda m: 'title: "' + m.group(1).strip() + '"',
            new_text, flags=re.MULTILINE)
        with open(f, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
            fh.write(new_text)
        changed_files.append(f)

print(f'Modified {len(changed_files)} files')
for f in changed_files:
    print(' -', f)
PYEOF

<script>
(function() {
  var filterEl = document.getElementById('lang-filter');
  if (!filterEl) return;

  function applyFilter(lang) {
    filterEl.querySelectorAll('.lang-filter-btn').forEach(function(b) {
      b.classList.toggle('active', b.dataset.lang === lang);
    });

    document.querySelectorAll('.blog-year-block').forEach(function(block) {
      var visibleCount = 0;
      block.querySelectorAll('.post-list-item').forEach(function(item) {
        var show = lang === 'all' || item.dataset.postLang === lang;
        item.style.display = show ? '' : 'none';
        if (show) visibleCount++;
      });
      block.style.display = visibleCount > 0 ? '' : 'none';
    });
  }

  filterEl.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
    var btn = e.target.closest('.lang-filter-btn');
    if (!btn) return;
    var lang = btn.dataset.lang;
    applyFilter(lang);
    var url = new URL(window.location);
    if (lang === 'all') { url.searchParams.delete('lang'); }
    else { url.searchParams.set('lang', lang); }
    history.replaceState(null, '', url);
  });

  // Deep-link support: /blog/?lang=en or /blog/?lang=my
  var requested = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get('lang');
  if (requested === 'en' || requested === 'my') {
    applyFilter(requested);
  }
})();
</script>
